problems.stem: A student submits the Module 6 package as a zip of six finished files: iteration log, AI-USE.md, quality review, theoretical defense, peer-critique responses, and slides. What separates a defensible package from this assembly?
options: The files should be PDFs, not a zip.
The components must tell one consistent story: the presentation's claims match the iteration log, the AI-USE.md, and the quality review.
There should be more than six files.
The files should be in alphabetical order.
problems.explanation: Completion is coherence, not assembly: a defensible package is internally consistent across its components, not just a folder of finished artifacts.

problems.stem: Your slides claim 'five rounds of learner testing,' but your iteration log records only two tryouts. What should you do before submitting the package?
options: Leave both as is; reviewers rarely cross-check components.
Reconcile the components so the claim and the log agree, correcting whichever is inaccurate.
Delete the iteration log so only the slides remain.
Add three more testing rounds to the slides to round it up.
problems.explanation: A committee will notice when the talk and the log disagree; cross-artifact claims must be reconciled before submission.

problems.stem: You ask an AI to write a one-page overview summarizing your whole capstone package. It states you 'conducted a formal usability study.' You ran informal tryouts. What is the correct boundary?
options: Submit the overview as written; it summarizes nicely.
Verify every statement in the AI overview against the real components and correct any that the artifacts do not support before submitting.
Replace your tryouts with the AI's description so they match.
Use the AI overview only and discard the underlying artifacts.
problems.explanation: An AI-assembled summary must be verified against each underlying artifact; submitting unverified claims you cannot defend undermines the package.

problems.stem: A reviewer says your completed package 'shows what you made but not what you learned.' Which addition best answers that?
options: A cover page with a larger title.
A synthesis tracing how your design judgment changed across the module and what you would do differently next time.
A second copy of each deliverable.
problems.explanation: A synthesis of how judgment evolved across the module turns a list of deliverables into evidence of learning the reviewer is asking for.
